chief_complaint: changing asymmetrical multicolored mole with irregular borders
hpi_details: A 26-year-old female presents to the clinic with changing asymmetrical multicolored mole with irregular borders. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks the mole became darker and irregular because she got sunburned on vacation and scratched it in her sleep.
concerns: She is worried that the changing mole is an aggressive skin cancer like the one her aunt passed away from a few years ago.
expectations: She hopes the doctor will examine the mole with a skin microscope and biopsy it today to give her a definitive answer.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Malignant Melanoma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

A suspicious pigmented lesion requires prompt complete excisional biopsy with narrow diagnostic margins when feasible; definitive excision margins and any sentinel-node discussion depend on Breslow thickness and other pathology.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

Key HPI features: A 26-year-old female presents to the clinic with changing asymmetrical multicolored mole with irregular borders. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Malignant Melanoma.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Malignant Melanoma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Dysplastic nevus without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Breslow depth predictors (ulceration, rapid vertical growth).
management_principles: Arrange prompt dermatology or surgical assessment for complete excisional biopsy when feasible; avoid partial sampling unless lesion location or size requires specialist planning.
After pathology, choose definitive excision margins and consider sentinel lymph node biopsy according to staging, Breslow thickness, ulceration, and patient factors.
Assess regional nodes and systemic symptoms and give clear follow-up and skin-surveillance advice.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: changing asymmetrical multicolored mole with irregular borders

A 26-year-old female presents to the clinic with changing asymmetrical multicolored mole with irregular borders. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Malignant Melanoma.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Malignant Melanoma.
reference_soap.plan: Arrange prompt dermatology or surgical assessment for complete excisional biopsy with narrow diagnostic margins when feasible. Do not select wide-excision margins or sentinel lymph node biopsy until histology and staging are available. Examine regional nodes and arrange urgent review for concerning systemic symptoms or rapidly progressive disease.

teaching.one_liner: Aggressive skin malignancy arising from melanocytes, requiring urgent excisional biopsy.
red_flags: Breslow depth predictors (ulceration, rapid vertical growth)

must_ask.say: Is the mole asymmetrical with irregular, notched, or blurred borders?
Does the mole contain multiple different colors like black, brown, red, or blue?
Has the spot grown larger than 6 millimeters or changed size, shape, or height recently?
Does the spot itch, bleed spontaneously, or form a crust?
Do you have a history of severe blistering sunburns or tanning bed use?

history.answer: I noticed a mole on my upper back has changed shape and color recently, and it is making me very worried.
I have had a tiny mole there for years, but over the past two or three months it started growing and looking completely different.
It is on my right upper back, just under my shoulder blade. My partner first pointed out that it looked strange.
It used to be a tiny flat speck, but over the last couple of months it expanded to about the size of a pencil eraser.
The borders are jagged and blurry, and the two halves do not match up at all.
It used to be a uniform light tan, but now it is mottled with dark brown, pitch black, and even a faint pinkish tint.
It has started to itch occasionally over the past few weeks, and it bled a little bit last week when my shirt rubbed against it.
There was a small crust after it bled, but it does not have a deep open sore or ulcer.
It feels slightly raised and a bit firmer than the surrounding skin, but it is not a hard knot stuck deep underneath.
No, it does not hurt at all, even when I press directly on it.
No, there is no redness spreading around it, no heat, and no pus or smelly drainage.
No, there is no central hole or pore, and nothing cheesy or white comes out of it.
No, it has never swollen up or shrunk back down; it has only gotten steadily bigger.
No, I have never had an injury, cut, surgery, piercing, or bad acne in that spot.
No, I have never tried to squeeze it, scratch it off, or put any over-the-counter wart or mole creams on it.

history.answer: I have normal scattered freckles on my shoulders, but none of them look dark, jagged, or changing like this one.
I used indoor tanning beds regularly for about two years during college, and I had several blistering sunburns as a teenager.
I checked under my arms and around my neck, and I have not felt any swollen glands or bumps.
No, I have not had any fevers, chills, or night sweats.
My weight has stayed the same, but I have been feeling unusually tired and run-down lately.
I thought the mole just got irritated and changed color because I got a bad sunburn on holiday and scratched it.
I'm really scared that this mole is a dangerous skin cancer, especially since my aunt passed away from one.
I do not have any chronic medical illnesses like high blood pressure, diabetes, or asthma.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or vitamins.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or latex.
No one in my family has had melanoma or any kind of skin cancer.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any vaping or tobacco products.
I only drink socially, maybe a glass of wine or beer once or twice a month.
I work indoors as an office administrator and live in an apartment with my partner.
My last period started two weeks ago, my cycles are regular every 28 days, and there is no chance of pregnancy.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.6 C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, well-nourished young female, appearing mildly anxious but in no acute distress.

On the right upper back, an 8 mm asymmetrical pigmented plaque with scalloped, irregular borders, variegated dark brown, black, and focal pink hues, and slight elevation; non-tender, non-indurated, freely mobile over deeper fascia, with no other suspicious pigmented lesions elsewhere on the skin.
No cervical, supraclavicular, or posterior triangle lymphadenopathy palpated.
No palpable axillary lymphadenopathy bilaterally, and no breast masses noted.
